If the Main and Child table is not existing then both get created during the 1st run  in the above set-up. If the Main table is already existing and the child table is added later , then the main table should be dropped . Re-run of the job will result in the creation/fill-up of both the tables

Note: Table Update to the Main table should be 'Add entries to table' , for users to be filled -in.

entry.title: Restricting User Access in SAP SuccessFactors via IAS & IPS Without Making the User Inactive
entry.content:
What This Blog Covers: A real-world implementation where a global organisation needed to restrict specific country-based users from accessing SAP SuccessFactors during a phased go-live rollout. We cover the complete journey — architecture, IPS transformation rules, IAS group management, conditional authentication, troubleshooting 10 real issues encountered, and how to cleanly remove restrictions post go-live. All sensitive information has been masked for publication.

1. Background and Business Requirement

During a phased go-live of SAP SuccessFactors (Recruiting, Onboarding, and Benefits modules), the requirement was to temporarily restrict users from a specific country entity from accessing the instance — while allowing all other global users to continue their normal SSO login via Microsoft Azure AD.

Key requirements:

#

Requirement

1

Restrict specific users based on their company/entity assignment in SuccessFactors

2

Keep restricted users active in IAS — no account deactivation

3

Non-restricted users must continue SSO via Azure AD without any disruption

4

Restriction must be temporary and easily reversible post Go-Live

5

Support both restricting all users in an entity AND specific named users

6

Work within the existing IAS + IPS + Azure AD SSO architecture

2. Solution Architecture

The solution connects SAP SuccessFactors, IPS, IAS, and Microsoft Azure AD. SAP SuccessFactors is the master source of users. IPS provisions users and group membership into IAS. IAS controls authentication routing and access decisions.

Component

Role in Solution

SAP SuccessFactors

Master source of users. Company/entity field (custom02) identifies restricted users.

IPS Source System

Reads users from SF, applies transformation rules, tags restricted users with IAS group

IPS Target System

Writes user attributes and group membership to IAS

IAS

Identity Provider for SP-initiated SSO. Applies access restriction rules.

Microsoft Azure AD

Corporate IdP used for Employee, Partner and Contractor SSO

IAS Group

Tags restricted users — referenced by Conditional Auth and Risk Based Auth rules

3. Solution Design — Three Layer Approach

The restriction requires all three layers working together. Removing any single layer causes the restriction to fail silently.

Critical: Without the Conditional Authentication Priority 1 rule, restricted users match the existing Employee/Partner rules and are routed directly to Azure AD — completely bypassing the Risk Based Auth DENY rule. All three layers are mandatory.

4. IPS Configuration

4.1 Identify the Company Field

The company/entity field in SF is mapped as custom02 in the IPS source transformation. The exact raw value must be verified from IPS trace logs — not the display label shown in the SF UI. Enable ips.trace.skipped.entity.content = true in IPS Source System Properties to see exact raw field values in provisioning logs.

Important: Always verify that custom02 is listed in the sf.user.attributes property of the IPS Source System. If missing, the SF OData API will never return this field and all custom02 conditions will silently fail with no error message shown.

4.2 Source Transformation — Three Approaches

Option A — Restrict all users in an entity (company field):

{    "condition": "$.custom02 == 'YOUR_COMPANY_CODE_VALUE'",    "constant": "Restricted_Users_Group",    "optional": true,    "targetPath": "$.groups[0].value"}

Option B — Restrict specific User IDs only:

{    "condition": "$.userId == 'USER_ID_1' || $.userId == 'USER_ID_2' || $.userId == 'USER_ID_3'",    "constant": "Restricted_Users_Group",    "optional": true,    "targetPath": "$.groups[0].value"}

Option C — Company entity with named exclusions (Recommended for large user sets):

{    "condition": "$.custom02 == 'YOUR_COMPANY_CODE_VALUE' && $.userId != 'EXCLUDE_USER_1' && $.userId != 'EXCLUDE_USER_2'",    "constant": "Restricted_Users_Group",    "optional": true,    "targetPath": "$.groups[0].value"}

Recommendation: Option C is best when you have a large number of users to restrict but a smaller exclusion list. It automatically applies to new hires in the entity and only requires maintaining the exclusion list — much shorter and more maintainable than listing hundreds of individual user IDs.

Note on userId: The userId field in IPS maps to the SF User ID field — NOT the Username or Login Name. These are completely different values. The userId is often numeric (e.g. 1103908). Always verify in SF Admin Center → Manage Users before using in conditions.

4.3 Target Transformation — Groups Passthrough Mapping

Add the following as the last mapping in the user section of the IAS target transformation (after the passwordStatus or sendMail mappings):

{    "sourcePath": "$.groups[*].value",    "preserveArrayWithSingleElement": true,    "optional": true,    "targetPath": "$.groups[?(@.value)]"} // Note: resolveEntityIds intentionally NOT used here.// Manually created IAS groups require direct passthrough.// resolveEntityIds silently drops group assignment when UUID not in IPS cache.

Do NOT use resolveEntityIds for manually created IAS groups. It silently drops the group assignment when the UUID is not in the IPS cache — no error is shown in provisioning logs.

4.4 Critical IPS Properties to Verify

Property

Required Value

Why It Matters

sf.user.attributes

Must include custom02

Without this, SF OData API never returns the field to IPS

sf.user.filter

status eq 'active'

Never filter to single user — causes mass deletion of all other IAS users

ips.trace.skipped.entity.content

true (for debugging)

Shows exact raw field values in provisioning logs

ips.trace.failed.entity.content

true (for debugging)

Shows full error details for failed entity provisioning

4.5 IPS Job Execution Sequence

Always follow this exact sequence. Skipping or reversing the order causes group assignment to fail silently with no error message.

1

Run READ job on IAS Source System

IPS → Source Systems → [IAS source system] → Jobs → Run Now → READ

Populates IPS internal UUID cache for IAS groups including the restriction group

2

Run RESYNC job on SF Source System

IPS → Source Systems → [SF source system] → Jobs → Run Now → RESYNC

Reads from SF AND writes to IAS. A READ-only job never writes to the IAS target

3

Verify Provisioning Logs

IPS → Provisioning Logs

Confirm restricted users show SUCCESS status

5. IAS Configuration

Group name is case sensitive — must exactly match the constant value in the IPS source transformation

5.3 Risk Based Authentication — Add DENY Rule

6. End-to-End Flow

User hits SF URL (SP-initiated SSO)

Non-Restricted User Login

7. Troubleshooting — Real Issues Encountered

Every issue below was encountered and resolved during the actual implementation. These are documented to help others avoid the same pitfalls.

#

Issue

Root Cause

Resolution

1

Group not populated in IAS after Resync

Groups passthrough mapping missing from target transformation user section

Add groups passthrough mapping in USER section of IAS target transformation

2

Groups mapping silently failing

resolveEntityIds cannot find UUID for manually created group

Remove resolveEntityIds from the groups mapping entirely

3

DENY rule not triggering

Conditional Auth routing user to Azure AD — DENY rule bypassed entirely

Add Priority 1 Conditional Auth rule routing restricted group to IAS native login first

4

User filter causing mass deletion in IAS

sf.user.filter set to single user — IPS flagged all other users for deletion

Always keep sf.user.filter = status eq 'active' — never filter to single user

5

READ job not updating IAS group

READ job only caches data internally — never writes to IAS target

Use RESYNC job which reads from SF AND writes to IAS target

6

userId condition not matching users

SF userId is often numeric — not the username or login name field

Verify exact userId in SF Admin Center → Manage Users before using in conditions

7

custom02 condition always fails

custom02 not listed in sf.user.attributes property — SF never returns the field

Add custom02 to sf.user.attributes in IPS Source System Properties

8

custom02 value mismatch

SF UI display name differs from the actual OData API raw value returned

Enable trace logging and check exact raw value in IPS provisioning logs

9

Password prompt instead of Access Denied

Risk Based Auth DENY evaluates only after the login attempt is submitted

Expected behaviour — users cannot authenticate regardless of password entered

10

IAS group still populated after removing IPS condition

IPS does not remove group membership when condition is removed — only adds or updates

Manually remove all members from IAS group OR delete the group entirely

8. Removing the Restriction (Post Go-Live)

Important: Removing the IPS condition does NOT automatically remove users from the IAS group. IPS only adds or updates group membership — it never deletes it. Manual removal of IAS group members is always required when lifting a restriction.

Step

Action

Details

1

Remove Group Rule from IPS Source Transformation

Delete the entire condition mapping block from the source transformation. Save the transformation.

2

Run IPS Jobs in Sequence

READ on IAS source → RESYNC on SF source. IPS will no longer re-add users to the group since the condition has been removed.

3

Manually Remove Group Members in IAS

IAS → Users & Authorizations → User Groups → Restricted_Users_Group → select all members → Remove. Alternatively, delete the group entirely if no longer needed.

4

Delete IAS Rules from All Applications

For every SF application in IAS, remove the Conditional Authentication Priority 1 rule AND the Risk Based Authentication DENY rule.

5

Verify SSO Works for Previously Restricted Users

Test 3–5 previously restricted users — they should now be redirected to Azure AD and login successfully via normal SSO.

9. Key Lessons Learned

#

Lesson

Why It Matters

1

Always run READ on IAS source BEFORE Resync

Populates IPS UUID cache needed for group resolution

2

Always use RESYNC job — not READ job

READ job only caches data internally and never writes to IAS target

3

Never filter sf.user.filter to a single user

Causes mass deletion of all other users in IAS on next Resync

4

No resolveEntityIds for manually created IAS groups

Silently drops group assignment with no error shown in logs

5

Conditional Auth Priority 1 rule is mandatory

Without it Azure AD authenticates users before DENY rule can fire

6

DENY rule belongs in Risk Based Auth — not Conditional Auth

Conditional Auth only routes users to IdPs — it cannot deny access

7

SF userId can be numeric — always verify exact value

The userId and Username fields are completely different in SF

8

custom02 must be listed in sf.user.attributes

Field never returned by SF OData API if not explicitly listed

9

IAS group name is case sensitive

Must match the IPS transformation constant value exactly

10

Removing IPS condition does not remove IAS group membership

Manual removal from IAS group is always required after lifting restriction

11

Groups mapping must be in USER section of target transformation

Group section may be set to ignore:true — placing mapping there has no effect

12

Use custom02 + exclusion list for large user sets

Shorter condition, auto-applies to new hires, much easier long-term maintenance

Summary: Restricting access in SAP SuccessFactors via IAS and IPS requires a three-layer approach — IPS transformation tags users with a restriction group, IAS Conditional Authentication routes them to IAS native login at Priority 1, and IAS Risk Based Authentication DENY rule blocks access. Users remain active in IAS throughout. The most critical insight: Conditional Authentication and Risk Based Authentication must work together — one routes the user, the other denies them. Neither works alone for this use case. When lifting the restriction, always manually remove members from the IAS group as removing the IPS condition alone does not trigger group membership deletion.

This blog documents a real implementation with real challenges encountered and resolved. Every troubleshooting point above was an actual issue from the project. I hope this helps others working on similar access restriction requirements with SAP SuccessFactors, IAS, and IPS. Feel free to leave questions in the comments!

entry.title: Understanding SuccessFactors SSO with IAS and IPS: A Simple Guide
entry.content:
Understanding SuccessFactors SSO with IAS and IPS: A Simple Guide

When people hear terms like SSO, IAS, IPS, SAML, and Identity Provider, the setup can sound complicated. In reality, the concept is quite simple.

This blog explains how users log in to SAP SuccessFactors using Single Sign-On (SSO) and how user accounts are synchronized automatically.

The Main Components

Before understanding the flow, let's understand the key systems involved.

1. SuccessFactors

This is the application employees use for HR activities such as leave requests, performance management, employee information, etc.

2. IAS (Identity Authentication Service)

IAS is responsible for authentication. It is the login gateway that verifies who the user is.

3. IPS (Identity Provisioning Service)

IPS is responsible for user synchronization and provisioning. It creates, updates, and manages user accounts across systems.

4. Corporate Identity Provider

This is the organization's central user directory, such as Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), ADFS, or another corporate authentication system.

What Is SSO?

SSO (Single Sign-On) allows users to log in once using their company credentials and access multiple applications without entering passwords repeatedly.

Instead of remembering separate passwords for SuccessFactors, employees simply use their corporate login.

What Is SAML?

SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is the technology that enables SSO.

Think of SAML as a digital verification letter.

Real-Life Example

Imagine entering a corporate office:

  1. Security checks your ID.
  2. Security gives you a visitor badge.
  3. Every department trusts that badge and allows entry.

In the same way:

  • Identity Provider = Security Desk
  • SAML Response = Visitor Badge
  • SuccessFactors = Office Building

The application trusts the badge issued by the trusted identity system.

Login Flow: Step-by-Step

Let's see what happens when an employee clicks the SuccessFactors URL.

Employee

↓

SuccessFactors

↓

IAS

↓

Corporate Identity Provider

↓

User Authenticated

↓

IAS

↓

SuccessFactors

↓

Access Granted

 

Step 1: User Opens SuccessFactors

The employee tries to access SuccessFactors.

Step 2: SuccessFactors Redirects to IAS

Instead of asking for a password, SuccessFactors redirects the user to IAS for authentication.

Step 3: IAS Redirects to Corporate Identity Provider

IAS sends the user to the organization's identity provider, such as Entra ID (Azure AD).

Step 4: User Authentication

The user enters corporate credentials.

The Identity Provider verifies:

  • Username
  • Password
  • MFA (if configured)

Once verified, the user is authenticated.

Step 5: SAML Response Is Created

The Identity Provider generates a SAML response and sends it back.

Example:

<NameID>ARAVIND.R</NameID>


The NameID is the most important attribute.

Step 6: IAS Validates the SAML Response

IAS checks:

  • Is the response coming from a trusted Identity Provider?
  • Is the digital signature valid?
  • Has the response been tampered with?

If everything is valid, IAS proceeds.

Step 7: SuccessFactors Identifies the User

SuccessFactors receives the authenticated user's information and searches for a matching username.

Example:

SuccessFactors User:

Username = ARAVIND.R

 

SAML Response:

<NameID>ARAVIND.R</NameID>

Result:

✅ Login Successful

This is why SAP recommends that the NameID value should match the SuccessFactors username.

What Happens If NameID Does Not Match?

Suppose:

SuccessFactors:

Username = ARAVIND.R

SAML Response:

<NameID>aravind@company.com</NameID>

SuccessFactors searches for:

Username = aravind@company.com

No matching user is found.

Result:

❌ Login Failure

Therefore, NameID mapping is one of the most important checks during SSO implementation.

Where Does IPS Fit In?

While IAS handles login, IPS handles user synchronization.

User Provisioning Flow

HR System / Active Directory

↓

IPS

↓

IAS

↓

SuccessFactors

Example

A new employee joins the company.

  1. HR creates the employee record.
  2. IPS reads the employee data.
  3. IPS provisions the user into target systems.
  4. IAS receives the user account.
  5. User can now log in to SuccessFactors.

Without IPS, administrators would need to create users manually.

Why Do We Exchange Metadata Files?

Before systems can trust each other, they exchange metadata files.

Metadata contains information such as:

  • Entity ID
  • SSO URLs
  • Certificates
  • Endpoints

SuccessFactors ↔ IAS ↔ Corporate Identity Provider

Think of metadata as an identity card exchanged between systems so they can recognize and trust each other.

What Is a Resync Job?

Sometimes source and target systems become inconsistent.

Example:

Source System : User Exists

Target System : User Missing

A Resync Job reads all users from the source and updates the target system to make both systems consistent again.

Think of it as:

"Refresh everything and rebuild the target system based on the source."

Complete Picture

Corporate Identity Provider

(Entra ID / Azure AD)

│

▼

IAS

Authentication

│

▼

SuccessFactors

 

▲

│

IPS

User Provisioning

│

▼

HR / AD Source System

 

Key Takeaways

✅ IAS is responsible for authentication and SSO.

✅ IPS is responsible for user provisioning and synchronization.

✅ SAML is the protocol that carries authentication information between systems.

✅ NameID in the SAML response should match the SuccessFactors username.

✅ Metadata exchange establishes trust between SuccessFactors, IAS, and the corporate Identity Provider.

✅ Resync Jobs help fix missing or inconsistent user data between systems.

Final One-Line Summary

IAS answers "Who are you?", IPS ensures "You exist in the system", and SuccessFactors provides the business application that the employee ultimately accesses.

 

Regards, 
Aravind Rajagopal,
SAP HXM Consultant

entry.title: Extending Case Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM: Using Business Roles for Multi-Users
entry.content:
This blog post is a continuation of: Assigning a Custom Party Role to a Case for Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM

Introduction

The previous blog post walked through how to create a Custom Party Role, add it to a Case Party Schema, and wire it into an Autoflow approval — a clean and effective pattern for routing a case to a named approver.

But what happens when your business scenario requires more than one approver? What if an entire team needs to approve a case, and that team membership changes over time?

SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 (SSC v2) and ESM do not have a native Branch or Approval Hierarchy construct the way some other products do. There is no built-in concept of "send to a department" or "broadcast to a group approval pool." You cannot pick a Business Role directly in the Approval Rule as a recipient group — the approval framework works with individual people assigned to the case.

This extension blog describes a practical pattern to bridge that gap:

Use a Business Role in SSC v2 as the governed container of approvers. Sync its membership from IAS via IPS over SCIM. Populate a non-unique Custom Party Role on the Case with all members of that Business Role. Then use the Case Approval flow to route to all those party role members simultaneously.

The result: a fully dynamic, centrally governed multi-user approval — without needing a branch or hierarchy model.

The Problem: No Branch, No Hierarchy, But Multiple Approvers Needed

In SSC v2/ESM case approvals, the approval process resolves its recipients from people assigned to a specific party role on the case. This works well for a single approver — assign one person to the "Line Approver" party role, and the approval goes to them.

However, real-world scenarios often require:

  • A team of approvers where any one member can take action (e.g., a support management pool)
  • A scenario where all members must approve (e.g., a compliance sign-off)
  • A quorum approval (e.g., at least 2 out of 5 approvers must accept)

And critically: approval team membership changes. People join, leave, change roles. Hardcoding names in configuration is not maintainable.

The answer lies in combining three capabilities:

  1. Business Roles in SSC v2 — as a group of approvers with a meaningful identity
  2. IAS User Groups + IPS SCIM provisioning — for centralized lifecycle management of who is in that group
  3. BTP Extensibility for Assignment of Users to Case from Business Role
  4. Non-unique Custom Party Role on the Case — as the runtime carrier of multiple approvers that the approval flow reads

Architecture Overview

IAS (Identity Authentication Service)
  └── User Group: "CASE_APPROVERS_GRP1"
       ├── User A
       ├── User B
       └── User C
          │
          │  IPS SCIM Sync (Business Role provisioning)
          ▼
SSC v2 / ESM
  └── Business Role: Z_CASE_APPROVERS_GRP1
       ├── User A (assigned this Business Role)
       ├── User B (assigned this Business Role)
       └── User C (assigned this Business Role)
          │
          │  Manual or Automated Party Assignment(BTP Extension)
          ▼
  Case → Custom Party Role: Z_GRP_APPROVER (non-unique)
       ├── User A (Party on Case)
       ├── User B (Party on Case)
       └── User C (Party on Case)
          │
          │  Autoflow → Approval Action
          ▼
  Approval Tasks sent to User A, User B, User C
  (All / Any One / At Least X — configurable)

Why This Pattern Works Without a Branch or Hierarchy

ChallengeHow It's Solved
No group/branch concept in approvalsBusiness Role acts as the group container; its members are loaded into a non-unique party role on the case
Approval team changes over timeIAS group membership is updated → IPS SCIM sync propagates changes to SSC v2 Business Role → Next case uses the updated team
Different cases need different approval groupsCreate one Business Role + Custom Party Role per approval group; populate the right one on each case based on conditions
Need any-one or all-must-approve semanticsControlled by the Approval Rule setting — no process redesign needed
Hardcoded user names in configurationNo user names anywhere in config — only role/group names

Summary

This pattern extends the Custom Party Role + Autoflow approval approach with a scalable, centrally governed layer. By treating a Business Role as the approval group, syncing its members from IAS via IPS over SCIM, and surfacing them on the case through a non-unique Custom Party Role, you unlock multi-user approval semantics in SAP SSC v2 / ESM — without needing any branch, hierarchy, or hardcoded user configuration.

The result is an approval flow that is:

  • Dynamic — membership changes in IAS flow through automatically
  • Flexible — supports any-one, all-must, or quorum approval modes
  • Maintainable — no user names in process configuration
  • Governed — IAS is the single source of truth for who approves what

Related blogs:

  • Assigning a Custom Party Role to a Case for Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM
  • Introducing SCIM API for SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2
  • Expanding SCIM API Support for SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2/ESM

entry.title: Why Manually Created Users Lose their Roles After SCIM Replication in SSCv2 +ESM— And How to Fix It
entry.content:
The Situation

Identity and access management in modern enterprise environments often involves a mix of provisioning strategies. In SAP's Sales & Service Cloud v2 (SSCv2) & SAP Enterprise Service Management (ESM), it is common to find tenants where some users are created manually by administrators while others are provisioned automatically through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management). This hybrid approach seems harmless — until you run a SCIM replication job and discover that manually created users have silently lost all of their assigned roles.

This is not a random glitch. It is a predictable, reproducible behavior rooted in how SCIM-enabled tenants manage role assignments — and understanding it is the first step to preventing it.

The Problem

In a SCIM-enabled SSCv2 tenant, users who were manually created (i.e., not provisioned through SCIM) and had business roles manually assigned to them lose those role assignments whenever a SCIM replication process runs — even though these users are not managed by SCIM at all.

What makes this particularly puzzling is that the Cloud Identity Service (CIS) logs show no record of updates to those manually created users during the replication run. From the system's perspective, nothing happened — yet the roles are gone.

How to Reproduce It

The issue is entirely reproducible. Here is the sequence of events that triggers it:

  1. Create a user manually in SSCv2 (outside of any SCIM provisioning flow).
  2. Assign one or more business roles to this user directly in SSCv2.
  3. Create a second user via SCIM provisioning from the Cloud Identity Service (CIS).
  4. Assign the same roles to the SCIM-managed user through CIS.
  5. Execute the SCIM replication process.
  6. Check the manually created user's role assignments.

Result: The manually created user's role assignments have been removed. The SCIM-managed user's assignments are intact. The CIS logs contain no trace of any action against the manually created user.

Why This Happens: The Root Cause

The behavior is not a bug in the traditional sense — it is a consequence of how role replication works in a SCIM-enabled tenant.

In SSCv2, when SCIM is enabled, the authoritative source for role assignments is Identity Authentication Service (IAS), not SSCv2 itself. The replication flow works as follows:

  • Roles are replicated from SSCv2 to IAS via replication jobs.
  • User-role assignments are replicated from IAS back to SSCv2 via those same jobs.

This means that during a replication run, SSCv2 does not selectively update only SCIM-managed users. Instead, it synchronizes role assignments based on what IAS reports. If a role is assigned to a SCIM-managed user in IAS, that assignment gets written to SSCv2. But because the manually created user has no corresponding record in IAS, the replication job effectively overwrites the role assignment state for that role — removing it from any user not represented in the IAS replication payload.

The silence in the CIS logs is explained by the same mechanism: CIS did not act on the manually created user. The removal is a side-effect of the IAS-driven synchronization overwriting what SSCv2 holds locally.

The Fix: Make Manually Created Users SCIM-Managed

The resolution is straightforward once the root cause is understood: manually created users need to become SCIM-managed users.

The recommended approach is to:

  1. Replicate the manually created users to IAS — either by re-creating them through the SCIM provisioning flow or by synchronizing them into IAS via the appropriate identity provisioning job.
  2. Allow IAS to replicate them back to SSCv2 so that SSCv2 recognizes them as SCIM-managed identities.

Once a user is SCIM-managed, the replication process treats their role assignments as part of the IAS-controlled state. Role assignments will no longer be removed during replication — they will instead be preserved and managed consistently alongside all other provisioned users.

What This Means in Practice

If your SSCv2 tenant is SCIM-enabled, the following rules of thumb apply:

ScenarioRisk
User created manually, roles assigned manuallyHigh — roles will be lost on next replication
User created via SCIM, roles assigned via CIS/IASSafe — roles are managed within the replication loop
User migrated to IAS and replicated back to SSCv2Safe — user is now SCIM-managed

The key principle: in a SCIM-enabled tenant, IAS is the source of truth for role assignments. Any role assignment that exists only in SSCv2 — without a corresponding entry in IAS — is at risk of being overwritten during the next replication cycle.

Recommendations

  • Audit your tenant for manually created users who have business roles assigned. These are the users at risk.
  • Do not mix provisioning strategies for the same set of roles. If a role is managed via SCIM, assume that all assignments for that role will be governed by the IAS replication process.
  • Migrate manually created users to IAS before the next replication run if they need to retain their role assignments.
  • Establish a governance policy that requires all new users in SCIM-enabled tenants to be created through the provisioning pipeline, not manually.
  • Monitor replication logs proactively — the absence of entries in CIS logs does not mean nothing changed in SSCv2.

The Golden Rule: SCIM Is a Day 1 Decision

If SCIM will ever be used in your SSCv2 tenant — even in the future — it must be architected from Day 1.

This is not a configuration preference. It is a foundational architectural decision with production consequences. Here is why:

Scenario RiskLevel Consequence
SCIM enabled before any user creationNoneAll users are provisioned consistently via IAS
SCIM enabled after manual users already existHighFirst replication job silently removes role assignments
Manual users migrated to IAS before next replicationMediumRecoverable — but requires careful, urgent remediation
Manual users NOT migrated before replication runsCriticalUsers lose access in production, no CIS log trace

Even if SCIM is not required at go-live, if there is any possibility it will be introduced later — plan for it now. The cost of retrofitting the provisioning model after manual users are established far exceeds the effort of doing it correctly from the start.

Summary

The loss of role assignments for manually created users in SSCv2 is not a random failure — it is the predictable outcome of a SCIM-enabled tenant architecture where IAS owns the user-role assignment state. The fix requires aligning manually created users with the provisioning model: replicate them to IAS and back to SSCv2, making them SCIM-managed. Once that alignment is in place, the replication process will preserve their role assignments rather than silently remove them.

If you are operating a hybrid environment where both manual and SCIM-provisioned users coexist, this issue is likely already affecting you. Addressing it proactively — before the next replication job runs — is far less disruptive than recovering from unexpected access loss in production.

 

Flow 1: The Problematic Scenario — SCIM Not Planned From Day 1

This is what happens when SCIM is introduced or enabled after users have already been created manually in SSCv2+ESM.

Key Insight: The damage is silent. CIS logs show nothing. The role removal is a side-effect of IAS overwriting SSCv2's local role assignment state — leaving no audit trail pointing to the affected users.

Flow 2: The Correct Approach — SCIM Planned From Day 1

This is the recommended architecture when going to production. SCIM must be the only provisioning channel from the very beginning.

entry.title: Migrate Data from SAP IDM via API
entry.content:
Migrate Data from SAP IDM via API

In my first post on SAP IDM data migration, I’ve introduced IDM CSV Server, an open source tool for replicating and migrating data from SAP Identity Management 8.0 to any next generation IAM solution. This is the second post on IDM CSV Server, and it is about publishing IDM CSV Server’s REST endpoints as an external API for scenarios where your data migration pipeline is in the public cloud. Specifically, I’ll go into detail on how to use Microsoft Entra ID as OAuth authorization server providing external authentication and authorization for the IDM CSV Server API.

Context and Companion Tutorial

The scenario related to this blog post is using SAP Integration Suite’s API management capability to publish an external API for IDM CSV Server. Covering this complete integration scenario in depth, however, is way more than what fits into one single article. I’ve therefore decided to focus this post on laying the required authentication and authorization groundwork. I’ll use Microsoft Entra ID as OAuth authorization server to create app registrations for IDM CSV Server and its CSV client, define an app role for the server and assign that to the client. After completing this groundwork, you’re free to complete the full scenario step-by-step by heading over to a separate, more extensive companion tutorial, which is available on Codeberg:

https://codeberg.org/freicoder/idm-server-csv-tutorial-api

The companion tutorial builds on the foundation we will create in Microsoft Entra ID over the course of this blog post. It contains detailed, end-to-end instructions for building, deploying and testing an API proxy for IDM CSV Server using SAP API Management (classic runtime/Apigee).

Scenario Overview

Use Case and Architecture

Our scenario is a migration project from SAP Identity Management 8.0 to a successor IAM solution from any vendor. In the tradition of my first post, I’ll generically call this successor NextGen IAM. Unlike in simpler SAP IDM migration scenarios where a one-time cutover from SAP IDM to another on premises IAM solution is sufficient, our particular scenario has two aspects that make it stand out:

  1. SAP IDM and NextGen IAM need to be operated in parallel for an extended period of time (weeks or months) for business reasons. During that period, their data needs to keep in sync. This is the ideal use case for IDM CSV Server, which makes data synchronization fast and repeatable specifically in SAP IDM migration projects.

  2. NextGen IAM is a public cloud solution with no direct network access to SAP IDM and SAP NetWeaver AS Java. Because IDM CSV Server runs on SAP NetWeaver AS Java, there’s no out-of-the-box solution for NextGen IAM to access IDM CSV Server. There are a number of different approaches for establishing a secure network link between public cloud and on premises SAP systems, such as SAP IDM. For the sake of our tutorial, we choose to build a custom API proxy for IDM CSV Server in SAP API Management to close the gap.

 

Scenario overview

In the center of our architecture is a data migration pipeline whose purpose is to retrieve person, role and assignment data from SAP IDM, process and transform that data and finally ingest the results into NextGen IAM. Technically, this data migration pipeline in the public cloud might be a Microsoft Azure Logic App.

Note that this migration scenario uses machine-to-machine (M2M) communication exclusively. The data migration pipeline executes periodically, e.g. hourly or daily, without any user interaction. Hence, pipeline components making outbound service requests require their own (non-human) client identity. This is true in particular for the custom CSV client, which periodically pulls data from SAP IDM.

In more conventional scenarios where IDM CSV Server is accessed from an on premises CSV client, HTTP basic authentication is the only available option. That’s not a secure choice for public cloud scenarios, however. It’s a better practice to use modern, secure authentication methods and hide SAP system internals, such as the credentials of SAP NetWeaver AS Java service users, from public cloud clients altogether. To this end, we’re going to build an API proxy in SAP API Management that requires clients to present an OAuth access token to be granted access to IDM CSV Server. OAuth 2.0, specifically its client credentials grant type, provides a secure and modern framework that enables clients in machine-to-machine scenarios to access protected resources on their own behalf - rather than on behalf of any specific human user. Without loss of generality, we’ll assume that the OAuth authorization server required by this architecture is provided by Microsoft Entra ID.

A Closer Look at Authentication and Authorization

The OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant type begins with the custom CSV client sending its client ID and client secret to the OAuth authorization server, in our case Microsoft Entra ID. In response to successful authentication, Entra ID returns an access token, which is a JSON Web Token (JWT). The CSV client then performs a second HTTP request, this time to the custom API proxy hosted in SAP API Management. The client sends the JWT received from Entra ID along with its HTTP request to the API proxy.

The API proxy verifies the JWT using a JSON Web Key (JWK), which it must fetch from Entra ID first. By verifying the JWT’s digital signature using the JWK, the API proxy confirms that the claims contained in the JWT can be trusted. After validating basic claims such as issuer and audience, the API proxy uses an additional claim (called “roles”) from the JWT to check whether this particular client is authorized to call IDM CSV Server. The rationale is to prevent that any authenticated client in possession of a valid access token from the trusted issuer is implicitly granted access to IDM CSV Server. Only clients explicitly authorized for this resource shall be granted access.

If the API proxy’s claims-based authorization check is successful, it sends a new, separate HTTP request to SAP Cloud Connector on premises, which in turn forwards that to the SAP NetWeaver AS Java backend. The API proxy does not forward the CSV client’s JWT in its own HTTP call. Instead, it uses HTTP basic authentication under the caller identity of a separate service user. This service user, which is managed by SAP NetWeaver AS Java, has been configured statically in SAP API Management at deployment time of the API proxy. Hence, there’s an identity context switch taking place in the API proxy at runtime - all calls to the backend or target endpoint will be made under one single caller identity. This switch to a pre-configured, static identity effectively cancels out IDM CSV Server’s built-in access control - all calls from API proxy to backend will be granted access. That’s why the API proxy needs its own, additional layer of authentication and authorization based on OAuth 2.0 on its front end side or proxy endpoint, as illustrated before.

Hands-On: Configuration Tasks in Microsoft Entra ID

Creating App Registrations in Microsoft Entra ID

We will create two app registrations for our scenario:

  1. One for the server side component providing protected resources, i.e. for IDM CSV Server
  2. One for the client side component requesting access to these resources, i.e. for the custom CSV client

To complete the following steps in your Microsoft Entra ID tenant, you’ll need authorized access to the Microsoft Entra Admin Center at

https://entra.microsoft.com

Your Entra ID user needs at least directory role Application Developer.

Creating the App Registration for the Server

Let’s start with the app registration for the server side. Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations and use the New registration button.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: New app registration for idm-csv-server

Provide a name, such as idm-csv-server, for the new app registration. Note that these names are not unique - there can be many app registrations with the same name. Leave Supported account types at its default Single tenant only. Do not provide any redirect URI. Use the Register button to save the app registration.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Save app registration for idm-csv-server

Adding an Application ID URI to the Server’s App Registration

The second step is to create an OAuth resource identifier, or application ID URI in Entra ID terms. This will be needed at runtime, first by the CSV client when requesting an access token from Entra ID for a specific scope, and subsequently by the API proxy in SAP API Management to validate the audience claim contained in the access token.

To create an application ID URI, find the entry Add an Application ID URI on the app registration’s Overview form or navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-server > Expose an API.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server

Use the Add button on the subsequent form Expose an API:

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server > Add

This will open the Edit application ID URI form, which will display the default application ID URI for this app registration. In Entra ID, the default value is api://<application (client) ID>, where application (client) ID is a GUID unique to this app registration.

GUIDs are hard to remember, so it might be tempting to change the default and define a custom application ID URI, such as api://idm-csv-server. I recommend you don’t do this, however.

Microsoft defines pretty strict syntax rules for application ID URIs, which are documented at https://aka.ms/identifier-uri-formatting-error. Unfortunately, easy to remember values like api://idm-csv-server don’t comply with these rules. Hence, I recommend staying with the default value. Before using the Save button, copy the application ID URI into the clipboard and save it locally for later use.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server > Save

You’ll need the application ID URI of idm-csv-server when working through the companion tutorial at two distinct points:

  1. in SAP API Management for configuring the API proxy after deployment using Key Value Maps (KVMs). The application ID URI of idm-csv-server goes into key jwtAudience of KVM IDM_CSV_SERVER_CONFIG.
  2. after completing deployment and configuration in SAP API Management for testing the integration scenario end-to-end. The application ID URI of idm-csv-server is part of the required value for IDM CSV Server Linux client’s command line parameter --oauth-scope.

Defining an App Role for the Server

Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations > idm-csv-server > App roles and use the Create app role button.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Create app role for idm-csv-server

On the Create app role form, enter a descriptive role name. Since this role, although defined by the server, is supposed to be assigned to the client, CSV Client is a suitable display name.

In the Allowed member types section, choose Applications. This is important because it is a prerequisite to be able to assign this app role to the second app registration for the client, which we will create shortly.

The string you enter in the third field, Value, is significant for authorization checks at runtime and hence by far the most important. The convention for app role values in Entra ID is <Resource>.<Operation>. For the server’s app registration, I recommend that you enter the following, case-sensitive string exactly as shown here:

 

IdmCsvServer.Invoke

It is this exact string that Entra ID will put into the roles claim of the access token. For a positive authorization decision, the string maintained here must be equal to what the API proxy in SAP API Management checks at runtime to decide whether the client is authorized to use IDM CSV Server or not.

Finally, enter something meaningful for the mandatory Description field and make sure to keep Do you want to enable this app role? checked, then use Apply to save your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Maintain app role value

Note that it is possible -although rarely required- to customize the app role value to something else. Keep in mind, however, that the app role value defined here, and the value checked in SAP API Management at runtime must match. Hence, if you decide to customize the app role value to something else here in Entra ID, make sure to also customize KVM key jwtClaimValue in SAP API Management to exactly the same value.

Creating the App Registration for the Client

Our next task is to create a second app registration, this time for the CSV client. While similar to what we have just done for the server, the procedure for the client differs significantly in two key aspects:

  1. Contrary to the server’s, the client’s app registration will require a client secret, enabling the client to authenticate with Entra ID at runtime - something the server never needs to do.
  2. Instead of defining a new app role, we’ll assign the server’s existing app role to the client’s app registration, thereby authorizing the client to invoke the server’s API.

Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations and use the New registration button. Use idm-csv-client as display name for this app registration.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: New app registration for idm-csv-client

Just as you did earlier for the server, leave Supported account types at its default Single tenant only and do not provide any redirect URI. Use the Register button to save the app registration.

Adding a Client Secret to the Client’s App Registration

To create a client secret, find the entry Add a certificate or secret on the app registration’s Overview form or navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-client > Certificates & secrets.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-server

Use the New client secret button on tab Client secrets of the subsequent form Certificates & secrets:

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > New

Provide a description and expiration period for the client secret, then use Add to save your changes. Note that Entra ID’s default expiration period of six months might be significantly longer than what most organizations will realistically need for migrating their data from SAP IDM to NextGen IAM, so it’s worth considering a shorter expiration period here.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > Save

Before pressing the Add button, make sure you have figured out a secure location, such as a vault or password manager, where to store the secret’s clear text value that will be displayed in the next step - recovering the cleartext value later on is not possible.

At runtime, the custom CSV client contained in the migration pipeline will need the combination of this client secret and the application (client) ID, which we’ll take care of next, to authenticate with Entra ID and obtain an access token. You’ll also need these values at the end of the companion tutorial to perform end-to-end tests.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > Copy

To obtain the application (client) ID, navigate back to this app registration’s Overview or alternatively Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-client > Overview. Find the entry called Application (client) ID and save that to your vault/password manager alongside the client secret saved earlier.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Copy client ID of idm-csv-client

Configuring Permissions of the Client’s App Registration

During creation of the server’s app registration, we defined a new app role whose value was IdmCsvServer.Invoke. Now we’ll assign this app role to the client’s app registration. OAuth distinguishes between delegated permissions for applications acting on behalf of a signed-in user and application permissions for applications acting on their own behalf. We’re discussing a machine-to-machine scenario here, so no signed-in user exists and delegated permissions are irrelevant. We’ll remove any delegated permissions which the client app registration got by Entra ID’s default, and assign IdmCsvServer.Invoke as application permission instead.

As we’ll see, this application permission assignment requires a two-step process: an application developer requests the assignment, and an application administrator approves or consents to, in OAuth terms, the assignment.

Removing Delegated Permissions from the Client’s App Registration

As stated above, our application doesn’t need any delegated permissions. However, every new app registration in Entra ID gets the delegated permission User.Read for Microsoft Graph API by default. While this doesn’t hurt our client from a functional perspective, we’ll remove the unneeded permission anyway on the grounds of principle of least privilege (PoLP).

Navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-server > API permissions.

In the Configured permissions section, verify that idm-csv-client currently has User.Read from category Microsoft Graph. Use the button labeled with three dots next to that category and select the Remove all permissions menu entry. The CSV client doesn’t use Microsoft Graph API at all, so we can safely remove all related permissions.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Remove delegated permission from idm-csv-client

Confirm the warning message claiming that these delegated permissions are required for proper application functionality - in our case, they are not. Use Yes, remove to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Confirm remove delegated permission from idm-csv-client

Requesting Application Permissions for the Client’s App Registration

Continue on the same form API permissions of idm-csv-client where you left off in the previous section and use Add a permission.

This will open a new form Request API permissions. Select the My APIs tab. In the list of applications displayed on this tab, find idm-csv-server - the server’s app registration which defines the permission we intend to assign to the client.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Expand API permissions defined by idm-csv-server

Click on idm-csv-server to display all API permissions (or app roles) defined by the server. Check the box next to IdmCsvServer.Invoke, then use Add permissions to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Request API permission defined by idm-csv-server for assignment to idm-csv-client

Verify that IdmCsvServer.Invoke is now being listed under Configured permissions and that its status is shown as Not granted for <your Entra ID tenant name>. Fixing this status is what we’ll take care of next.

Granting Admin Consent for the Requested Application Permissions: Prerequisites

As explained earlier, M2M scenarios cannot use interactive permission request and consent at runtime because there’s no signed-in user. Hence, consenting to permission requests is something a dedicated application administrator must do before the application can successfully execute. This application administrator will need to consent to this permission request not only for himself or any specific end user, but rather for all users - in other words, for the complete Entra ID tenant. Giving such administrative approval is what is commonly referred to as granting admin consent in OAuth terms.

If you’ve followed my instructions verbatim and currently use the Microsoft Entra Admin Center as a user who merely has directory role Application Developer, you’ll notice that the button Grant admin consent for <your Entra ID tenant name> is disabled, as shown in the following screenshot - you’re not authorized to use that function.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent disabled for application developer

That’s by design, because this request/approve workflow is designed with segregation of duties (SoD) in mind. Unless you have a privileged Entra ID user account on your own, you’ll need to ask your responsible Entra ID administrator to take over the remaining approval steps.

Eligible Entra ID administrators will need at least one of the following two directory roles to be able to grant admin consent:

  • Cloud Application Administrator (recommended)
  • Application Administrator

Assignment to the directory role will typically need to be activated using Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) at https://aka.ms/pim first, as illustrated next.

Use the Activate button next to Cloud Application Administrator to open a new form where you’ll need to provide at least a Reason for assignment activation. Finally, use the Activate button on that second form to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Activate Cloud Application Administrator Role

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Finalize Activation of Cloud Application Administrator Role

Assignment to Cloud Application Administrator will be activated asynchronously. After a couple of seconds, a UI message should inform you that your set of active assignments has changed. Switch to the Active assignments tab in PIM and verify that the assignment is now in state Activated.

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Verify Activation of Cloud Application Administrator Role

Granting Admin Consent for the Requested Application Permissions: Execution

Sign in to Microsoft Entra Admin Center at https://entra.microsoft.com using the privileged Entra ID user account who has an active assignment to directory role Cloud Application Administrator. Navigate to Entra ID > App registrations. Switch to the All applications tab and find idm-csv-client, keeping in mind that this display name is not unique. In case you have been experimenting and trying different things out, like I did, you may see more than one match when searching by display name. If in doubt, use the application (client) ID of idm-csv-client you noted down previously. This application (client) ID is unique, and you can use it to search just like the display name.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Find App Registration By Application (Client) ID

Click on the matching idm-csv-client entry, then navigate to its API permissions form. You’ll notice that the button Grant admin consent for <your Entra ID tenant name> is enabled, now that you are signed-in with a sufficiently privileged user. Use that button now and confirm the subsequent dialog with Yes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent > perform

Verify that the status of the requested application permission has changed from Not granted for … to Granted for ….

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent > verify

Wrap Up and Next Steps

Congratulations, you’ve completed all configuration required in Microsoft Entra ID. We can now use Entra ID as OAuth authorization server in an integration scenario for secure data migration from SAP IDM on premises into the public cloud. Your key takeaways from this blog are the following three important configuration properties, whose values you will need for the CSV client’s runtime:

  1. Application ID URI of idm-csv-server
  2. Application (client) ID of idm-csv-client
  3. Client secret of idm-csv-client

As you saw, the material discussed here was in many respects a cross-cutting topic at the intersection between integration and security concerns, and also between the SAP and Microsoft worlds. I hope readers interested in either or all of these fields found it worthwhile.

If you enjoyed the content presented here and wish to continue implementing the complete integration scenario end-to-end, I encourage you to head over to my companion tutorial on Codeberg. As mentioned in the introduction, the tutorial picks up from where this blog post leaves off and dives into SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector in more detail. By the end of the tutorial, you will be able to fetch CSV exports from an on-premises SAP IDM via a secure, internet facing API that uses OAuth for authentication.

Have fun, happy hacking!

entry.title: SAP IDM insights: Provisioning queue stuck
entry.content:
Some quick tips and Insights 

1. Make all dispatchers stop and start. if this does not resolve, try below in order

2. Stop all dispatchers other than allocated for provisioning. Restart the Provisioning dispatcher

3.  Check if the below views have entries. These views pick up records from mxp_provision and then are handed over to the respective dispatcher.. Eg. Ordered tasks are picked up by the Provisioning dispatcher.

MXPV_GROUPTASKS - parent/final

 

  • MXPV_GROUPTASKS_APPROVAL
  • MXPV_GROUPTASKS_ATTESTATION
  • MXPV_GROUPTASKS_CONDITIONAL
  • MXPV_GROUPTASKS_ORDERED
  • MXPV_GROUPTASKS_SWITCH

MXPV_GROUPTASKS  have the final list of records to be processed by the dispatcher. 

4. In order to stop all other records(except belonging to MXPV_GROUPTASKS_ORDERED) from being picked by the dispatcher, the state of the records can be made to something like 200(any value not in mxp_state). This can be done using the update  command on the mxp_provision and mxp_audit table. Unless this Audit table is updated with the state(Eg. 200), the records will get picked up by the dispatcher .
5. Sometimes if there are old records which need to be cleaned up from provisioning queue then make the status in mxp_audit table either as failed(1001)/success(1000). The status values can be obtained from mxp_provstatus.

And then delete the same from mxp_provision table using the delete from where clause.

entry.title: Identity and Access Management with Microsoft Entra, Part IV: Integration with SAP Cloud IAG
entry.content:
This scenario extends the architecture introduced in part III by shifting responsibility for provisioning SAP role assignments from SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS), Identity Provisioning, to SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG). Microsoft Entra ID Governance manages the access package and its assignment lifecycle, while SAP IAG applies SAP-specific approval workflows, risk controls, and downstream role provisioning. The scenario introduces the new SAP IAG connector in Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Azure Key Vault for securely storing the credential when calling the SAP IAG REST API.

 

Note 📢

Interested in connecting with us and discuss your SAP and Entra scenario? Then join the SAP and Microsoft identity teams at SAP TechEd 2026 in Berlin, and add hands-on session XP263 to your event agenda, where you will learn how SAP Cloud Identity Services, SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance, and Microsoft Entra work together to unify user lifecycle management and governance across SAP and third-party application.

Scenario Overview

The architecture for part IV builds on the identity provisioning scenario introduced in part III of this blog series. Microsoft Entra ID remains the central service ("source of authority", SOA) for identity data, and SAP CIS continues to receive users from Microsoft Entra and provisions them to downstream SAP target systems, such as the SAP system on-premises in the corporate network shown in figure 1.
Figure 1: Scenario Overview

 

However, responsibility for provisioning application access to the SAP backend system changes. In part III, SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Provisioning created the backend roles as groups in Microsoft Entra configured as a target system, and translated group memberships provisioned with the Entra SCIM-based SAP CIS provisioning connector into role assignments in the SAP backend system.

In this new scenario, SAP IAG takes over responsibility for governing and provisioning the user’s role assignment to the SAP backend system. Instead of directly translating a Microsoft Entra group assignment into an SAP role assignment, Microsoft Entra now requests access to an SAP IAG business role. SAP IAG processes the access request, applies the configured approval workflow and access controls, and provisions the underlying technical role to the target SAP backend system.
This separation allows each platform to focus on its core capabilities:
  • Microsoft Entra ID Governance provides the entitlement catalogs, access packages, request policies, and the user-facing Microsoft My Access portal.
  • SAP IAG provides SAP business roles, SAP-specific access request workflows, access analysis, risk evaluation, mitigation controls, and provisioning to connected SAP applications in the Cloud and on-premises.
  • SAP CIS maintains the shared user identities and supports identity synchronization between Microsoft Entra and SAP IAG.
  • SAP BTP connectivity service and SAP Cloud Connector provide the technical connection from SAP IAG to the SAP backend system on-premises.
From all components and configurations marked as "new" in figure 1, the SAP IAG tenant is the most important addition to the architecture in this scenario. SAP IAG maintains the business roles that can be requested through Microsoft Entra and maps those business roles to technical roles in connected SAP applications.
In the example scenario, the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the SAP ABAP system A4H. This business role is included in a new Microsoft Entra access package SAP EPM IAG and requested by the user Linda Larson. Microsoft Entra does not provision the underlying ABAP role directly. Instead, Microsoft Entra creates an access request in SAP IAG by calling the SAP IAG Access Request Service API. SAP IAG processes the request and, after the configured workflow has completed successfully, provisions the technical role to the target system.
SAP CIS Identity Provisioning remains part of the wider landscape, particularly when SAP IAG connects to supported cloud applications through Identity Provisioning proxy systems. However, SAP IAG now governs the access decision and orchestrates the provisioning operation for the requested SAP business role.
For this integration, Microsoft Entra ID Governance introduces an SAP IAG connector. The connector establishes the integration between Microsoft Entra entitlement management and the SAP IAG tenant. The connector enables administrators to:
  • Add an SAP IAG tenant as a resource to a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog
  • Discover SAP IAG business roles
  • Add SAP IAG business roles to Microsoft Entra access packages
  • Create SAP IAG access requests when an access package is assigned
  • Initiate removal requests when an assignment expires or is revoked
  • Retrieve the processing status of SAP IAG access requests
All of the actions above will be executed in the exercises of this blog series scenario. The connector communicates with SAP IAG through the Access Request Service REST APIs and authenticates by using OAuth 2.0 client credentials which require a secure storage option offered by the Azure Key Vault service to store the SAP IAG API OAuth client secret used by the SAP IAG connector. When configuring the connector in Microsoft Entra, the administrator selects the Azure subscription, Key Vault, and secret. The SAP IAG client ID, OAuth token URL, and SAP IAG API URL are configured as additional connector properties coming from the service key created for the SAP IAG API service instance in the SAP BTP subaccount.
 
SAP CIS remains essential to this scenario. Microsoft Entra provisions users to the Identity Directory in the SAP CIS tenant through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, RFC 7644). These users and their identifiers are subsequently synchronized into the SAP IAG repository. The Microsoft Entra user's globally unique object ID is mapped to the SAP Global User ID to provide a stable identity correlation across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG. Manager information must also be synchronized when SAP IAG workflows use the user’s manager as an approver. The scenario therefore governs role access for existing users who must already exist in SAP CIS and in the SAP IAG repository before Microsoft Entra submits the SAP IAG access request.
The target SAP applications must be registered and connected to SAP IAG. The provisioning mechanism depends on the application type:
  • For an on-premises system like the SAP Application Server ABAP, SAP IAG uses an SAP BTP destination, the SAP Connectivity service, SAP Cloud Connector, and the required BAPI or RFC interfaces.
  • For supported cloud applications, SAP IAG can use SAP Identity Provisioning proxy systems and the IPS_PROXY destination configured in the BTP subaccount.
The five steps shown in the scenario diagram of figure 1 illustrate the complete access governance process:
  1. Microsoft Entra provisions the users required in SAP IAG (Linda Larson, Tina Johnson & your Entra administrator user) and their SAP IAG roles as group memberships to SAP CIS through the existing enterprise application and SCIM provisioning connection (Note: inbound- or HR-driven provisioning of the test users in this scenario from SAP SuccessFactors to the corporate Active Directory and from there to Entra does not change from the scenario in part III of this blog series). The provisioning configuration must synchronize the Microsoft Entra object ID of the users as the SAP Global User ID. Manager information must also be synchronized if the SAP IAG workflow uses manager-based approval. In this scenario, Tina Johnson is assigned in Active Directory as the manager of Linda Larson and can approve Linda's access request in SAP IAG. After provisioning from Entra to SAP CIS is complete, the relevant SAP IAG synchronization jobs must import the user, groups, and identifiers from SAP CIS into SAP IAG's user repository. All users must be available in SAP IAG before an access request can be submitted from Microsoft Entra.
  2. Linda Larson opens the Microsoft My Access portal and requests the SAP EPM IAG access package. The access package is maintained in a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog and contains the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM.
  3. The SAP IAG connector calls the SAP IAG APIs and creates an access request for the user and selected business role. SAP IAG validates the request and that the user exists in its repository.
  4. SAP IAG processes the request according to the workflow and governance configuration of the SAP IAG tenant. Depending on the organization’s configuration, processing can include manager approval, segregation of duties (SOD) analysis, critical access analysis, assignment of mitigation controls and other steps. In this scenario, Tina Johnson as the manager of Linda Larson needs to approve Linda's access request. Microsoft Entra governs eligibility for the access package and its assignment lifecycle. SAP IAG governs the SAP-specific role assignment and applies SAP-specific risk and compliance controls.
  5. After the SAP IAG workflow has completed successfully, SAP IAG provisions the business role to the connected target applications. In the scenario, the business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the ABAP system A4H. SAP IAG uses the configured SAP BTP destination to reach the target system through SAP Cloud Connector and invokes the required BAPIs. The result is the assignment of SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO to Linda Larson's user in the SAP backend system.

For a live demo, check out episode #307 of the SAP on Azure video podcast, where @Holger-Bruchelt and I go through the scenario step by step.

Microsoft Entra continues to manage the lifecycle of the access package assignment. If the assignment expires or is revoked, Microsoft Entra uses the SAP IAG connector to initiate a removal request. SAP IAG processes that request and deprovisions the corresponding role from the target system. As part of the following exercises, the Microsoft Entra tenant administrator removes Linda's assignment to the SAP EPM IAG access package to test deprovisioning in the scenario.

entry.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2:Setting Up Principal Propagation with OAuth2SAMLBearer Authentication
entry.content:
This is my 350th blog post, and I'm excited to continue sharing insights, experiences, and lessons learned with the community.

Introduction

When integrating SAP BTP services with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 or SAP Service Cloud Version 2 or ESM, one of the most common requirements is ensuring that the identity of the logged-in user flows seamlessly from the source BTP application into the target SAP Cloud system. This is known as Principal Propagation.

Without principal propagation, every API call would authenticate as a technical/service user — losing all user context, audit trails, and authorization logic that depends on who is actually logged in. With it, the end user's identity is securely carried through, enabling fine-grained access control and meaningful audit logs on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud side.

This blog walks you through the complete setup using the OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow — the recommended approach for BTP-to-SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 connectivity.

How It Works — The Big Picture

User (logged into BTP app)
        │
        ▼
BTP Destination (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)
        │  ── Generates a SAML assertion carrying the user's identity
        ▼
SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 Token Service
        │  ── Validates the assertion against the trusted certificate
        ▼
Returns an OAuth2 Access Token (scoped to that user)
        │
        ▼
API Call executed as the propagated user
The trust between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 is established by registering BTP's X.509 certificate as a trusted issuer inside the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant.

Prerequisites

  • Access to your SAP BTP Cockpit (subaccount level)
  • Admin access to your SAP Sales Cloud V2 / Service Cloud V2 tenant
  • Ability to call REST APIs on the tenant (e.g., via Postman, Bruno, or curl)

Step 1: Download the BTP Trust Certificate

  1. Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your subaccount.
  2. Go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust (top-right area of the Destinations page).
  3. A .pem certificate file will be downloaded.
  4. Open the file and copy only the certificate content — the block between (but not including) the header and footer lines:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIEXzCCA0...   ← copy everything between these lines
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

Keep this certificate value handy — you'll need it in the next step.

Step 2: Configure Inbound OAuth2 Trust in SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2

SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 needs to know about BTP as a trusted SAML assertion issuer. This is done via a dedicated IAM Service REST API on your tenant.

Important restriction: Only one OAuth2 SAML Bearer Inbound Configuration can exist per tenant.

2a. Check if a Configuration Already Exists

Send a GET request to check the current state:

GET <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
  • If a configuration exists with the same BTP certificate → you can reuse it as-is.
  • If a configuration exists with a different certificate → update it (Step 2b).
  • If no configuration exists → create a new one (Step 2c).

2b. Update an Existing Configuration (PUT)

PUT <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration/34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "<existing Id found in Step 2a>",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2c. Create a New Configuration (POST)

POST <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2d. Save the Response Values

A successful POST or PUT returns a JSON response like this:

{
  "value": {
    "id": "...",
    "grantType": "SAML2_BEARER",
    "nameIdType": "EMAIL",
    "spEntityId": "...",
    "audience": "<AUDIENCE>",
    "tokenServiceUrl": "<TOKEN_URL>",
    "clientId": "<CLIENT_ID>",
    "scopes": ["<SCOPE_ID>"],
    "clientAppName": "...",
    "certificate": "..."
  }
}

Note down these four values — you'll need them in Step 3:

Field Used As

audienceAudience in BTP destination
tokenServiceUrlToken Service URL in BTP destination
clientId → appears as CLIENT_IDClient Key in BTP destination
scopes[0] → SCOPE_IDScope in BTP destination

Step 3: Create the BTP Destination

Now configure a destination in your BTP subaccount that uses the inbound configuration values you just collected.

  1. Go to SAP BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination.
  2. Fill in the following fields:

Property Value

NameYour choice (e.g., SalesCloudV2_PrincipalProp)
TypeHTTP
URL<Your SAP Sales/Service Cloud Tenant Host URL>
AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
Audience<AUDIENCE> from the inbound config response
AuthnContextClassRefurn:none
Client Key<CLIENT_ID> from the inbound config response
Token Service URL<TOKEN_URL> from the inbound config response
Scope<SCOPE_ID> from the inbound config response
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

The nameIdFormat value tells the system to use the user's email address as the SAML NameID — this is how the user identity is matched on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 or ESM side.

Step 4: Configure Trusted Domains in SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management

As a final step, ensure that your SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant domain is registered as a trusted domain in SAP BTP's Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA/SAP Cloud Identity Services).

Refer to the official SAP documentation: Configure Trusted Domains for SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service.

This ensures that SAML assertions issued by BTP are only accepted by explicitly trusted target systems — an important security boundary.

Summary

Here's a quick recap of the end-to-end setup:

Step 1 → Download BTP X.509 Trust Certificate
Step 2 → Register certificate as Inbound OAuth2 Config on SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2
Step 3 → Create OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Destination in BTP using response values
Step 4 → Register SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 domain as trusted in BTP Auth & Trust

Once complete, any BTP application or service using this destination will automatically propagate the logged-in user's identity to SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 — without requiring users to re-authenticate or sharing technical credentials.

Key Takeaways

  • Principal Propagation bridges the identity gap between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2, preserving the real user context across systems.
  • The trust is certificate-based — BTP's signing certificate is registered directly in the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 IAM service.
  • The fixed UUID (34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667) is a well-known system identifier for this configuration — don't change it.
  • Only one inbound configuration is allowed per tenant, so manage it carefully across teams.
  • User matching relies on email address as the SAML NameID — ensure users exist with the same email in both systems.

Share to your colleagues or Have questions or ran into issues during the setup? Drop them in the comments below.
